title: Cloudflare Tests Cache Transcoding to Reduce Storage Requirements
gist: Cloudflare is prototyping 'Cache Transcoding,' which Zstandard-compresses uncompressed cacheable text (HTML/JSON/CSS/JS) once on ingest, cutting eligible content size by about 2.8x and unlocking petabytes of effective cache capacity for a small CPU cost, while deliberately skipping already-compressed media that dominates byte volume.

insights.claim: Cloudflare's Cache Transcoding prototype compresses eligible cache content once when it enters the cache using Zstandard and decompresses it when served, with the encoding cost paid a single time while storage and bandwidth savings recur on every subsequent reuse of that asset.
insights.speaker: Aashi Patel (Cloudflare, cited by Renato Losio)
insights.so_what: A one-time compression cost with compounding reuse savings is a favorable economic pattern for high-traffic CDN caches — the more cache-hit reuse, the better the ROI, which scales naturally with popular content.
insights.quote: A small increase in CPU gives Cloudflare petabytes of effective cache capacity and reduces the data transferred between our data centers. The encoding cost is paid once when an asset enters the cache. The storage and bandwidth savings continue every single time that asset is reused.

insights.claim: Compression reduced the size of eligible content by about 2.8 times, and Cloudflare estimates the approach could provide petabytes of additional effective cache capacity across its infrastructure, though broader testing is still needed before wider rollout.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A 2.8x compression ratio applied at CDN scale translates into material infrastructure cost avoidance (fewer disks/servers needed for the same effective cache capacity) — relevant for evaluating Cloudflare's infrastructure capex trajectory and margin profile.
insights.locator: Compression reduced the size of eligible content by about 2.8 times

insights.claim: Cache Transcoding is built on Zstandard (Facebook's lossless real-time compression algorithm) combined with Pingora, Cloudflare's Rust-based proxy framework, integrating compression directly into the request-serving path.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Shows Cloudflare's continued reliance on its Rust-based Pingora proxy as core infrastructure for performance-sensitive features, reinforcing Pingora's strategic importance beyond its original open-sourcing as a proxy framework.
insights.locator: To achieve this, Cloudflare relies on Zstandard

themes.theme: Selective compression: what gets transcoded and why

insights.claim: Cache Transcoding only compresses uncompressed responses containing compressible text that return successfully and are at least 4 KiB, excluding range requests, precompressed or binary content, and responses of unknown size; this 4 KiB threshold sacrifices only about 1% of otherwise-eligible data while avoiding wasted CPU on many small objects.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A concrete, tunable size-threshold design pattern (4 KiB, ~1% data sacrificed) for balancing compression CPU overhead against capacity gains — a reusable engineering benchmark for any team building similar cache compression systems.
insights.locator: Cloudflare's Cache Transcoding only compresses uncompressed responses

insights.claim: Cloudflare deliberately excludes images, video, and fonts from transcoding because they are usually already compressed; in Cloudflare's traffic sample, this media slice represented 21.4% of requests but 63.3% of bytes, so compressing it again would burn CPU for no gain.
insights.speaker: Aashi Patel (Cloudflare, cited by Renato Losio)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the traffic composition insight driving the feature's design: most bytes (63.3%) are media that's not worth touching, so the compression effort concentrates on the smaller-byte-share but still substantial text traffic — a useful benchmark for anyone estimating similar cache economics.
insights.quote: In our traffic sample, this media slice represented 21.4% of requests but 63.3% of bytes. Compressing it again would burn CPU for nothing.

insights.claim: Compressible text such as HTML, JSON, CSS, and JavaScript accounted for 67.3% of requests but only 22.3% of bytes in Cloudflare's traffic sample, and of that content about 71% arrived uncompressed and could be effectively compressed by the new system.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Reveals that a majority of web requests (67.3%) are small text assets often served uncompressed (71% of them) — a data point useful for any CDN/edge infrastructure vendor benchmarking their own compression coverage against Cloudflare's findings.
insights.locator: According to Cloudflare, compressible text such as HTML, JSON, CSS, and JavaScript

themes.theme: Open technical questions and community pushback

insights.claim: Some practitioners on Hacker News questioned Cloudflare's use of the term 'transcoding' for what is essentially an encode/decode compression approach, while others debated the compression strategy itself, including whether cold (less popular) content rather than all eligible content should have been prioritized for compression to save CPU during decode.
insights.speaker: MayeulC (Hacker News commenter, cited by Renato Losio)
insights.so_what: Community skepticism about terminology and prioritization strategy signals the feature is still in early, debated design stages — not yet a settled architecture, so specifics may still change before general availability.
insights.quote: Weird, I would have compressed cold content instead, if the goal was to save on CPU time during decode.
insights.locator: As Cloudflare initially considered limiting transcoding to popular content

insights.claim: A Hacker News commenter raised an unresolved question about how range requests are handled under Cache Transcoding, since without compression such requests can be served by reading just the relevant part of a cached file, but compression complicates that direct byte-range access.
insights.speaker: CodesInChaos (Hacker News commenter, cited by Renato Losio)
insights.so_what: An open technical gap (range request handling under compression) that Cloudflare has not fully addressed publicly — worth monitoring for how it's resolved, given range requests are common for video/large file streaming.
insights.quote: I'm confused by how this affects range requests. Without compression, those can be easily satisfied by reading the relevant part of the cached complete file. But how are they handled now?

insights.claim: Cloudflare tested the prototype both with and without Tiered Cache to measure compression's impact on local caching and inter-tier transfers, and states the prototype remains under development with further testing planned across compression levels, content types, object sizes, and cache scenarios.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Confirms this is an early-stage prototype, not a shipped production feature — investors/engineers should treat the 2.8x compression and petabyte-capacity figures as preliminary estimates subject to change.
insights.locator: Tests were performed with and without Tiered Cache
